angle: Movement translation (DL, the group with the clearest signal of five screened): each rusher's tracked Combine 40 start curve (speed every 0.1 s from first movement, 0-1.5 s) laid over his own random NFL pass-rush starts from game_frames_sample on the same time axis. Translation is measured tenth by tenth, raw and after weight and role. The per-player Carry-over (NFL first step minus Combine first step, sd after weight and role) is tested against pressure rate beyond draft pick, in sample, out of class and as a calibration against the no-tracking forecast.
metric_name: Carry-over: NFL first step (mean speed 0.3-0.5 s after first movement on random NFL pass-rush starts, adjusted for alignment) minus Combine 40 first step (same window, year-standardized), each in sd after weight and EDGE share
headline_number: Raw, the 40 previews NFL speed at 1.5 s at rho 0.57; after weight and role the figure is -0.02 [90%: -0.24, 0.19], and for the first step it is 0.07 [-0.14, 0.28] (n = 67 DL). Carry-over vs pressure beyond pick, weight and role is 0.18 [-0.10, 0.44] (n = 52), and the held-out R2 change is -0.114. The NFL first step alone gives 0.22 [0.01, 0.43] (n = 69) but fails out of class (-0.113 [-0.311, 0.026]) and is dominated by NGS get-off (0.40). Top-third first-step rushers beat the out-of-class forecast 61% of the time (exact 90% interval 42-78%), against 13% for the bottom third.
what_changed_from_previous: New take on the translation angle (round 7 cand_3 scored 7.83 with the Film Equivalent launch metric). (1) A tracking-native design: whole speed-vs-time curves on one time axis, both in the hero (four named rushers, one per quadrant, Combine and NFL traces overlaid, with a pressure-vs-forecast bar for each) and in Figure 2 (translation and payoff tenth by tenth). (2) A new and stronger football finding: the apparent 40-to-Sunday carry-over (0.57) is weight; after weight and role it is about zero at every tenth, the pass-rush drill does no better, and the stopwatch 40 time beats the tracked start. (3) Applies the judges' round-7 changes: one metric name; a ~60-word lede; a why-now beat; a 3-row summary table; a decision card of 8 named rushers with one plain call each (2025 rows marked as the clean check, Maason Smith shown as the counter-example); raw pressure rates and beat-forecast shares by quadrant and by EDGE vs interior; leave-one-class-out calibration with exact binomial intervals plus a 2025-only line; selection made explicit (5 similarity definitions reported, a max-over-13-windows permutation p = 0.12, group chosen from 5); out-of-class figure rows labelled with held-out class and n; claims.json maps every numbers.json key to its sentence. (4) Every number is rendered from numbers.json by the analysis script (about 20 s runtime). 1,902 words, 4 figures and 3 tables; check.py passes.
open_risks: The headline is a null for production: carry-over, Combine first step and NFL first step all lower held-out R2 (2024 is strongly negative, driven by Maason Smith), so judges may read it as another 'tracking adds ~0' audit

The only positive signal (NFL first step, 61% vs 13% beat-forecast) is in sample except for its out-of-class forecasts, and NGS get-off already captures it (0.40; ours adds 0.12 beyond it). The first-step window was read off the payoff curve (max-T p = 0.12)
The first-step window (0.3-0.5 s) and onset anchoring are design choices; the first three tenths are set by the onset rule and are excluded from the curves
OL, DB and TE NFL starts have reliability of 0.20 or less on 20 random snaps, so the five-group screen mainly shows those groups cannot be read; DL was chosen after looking
No blockers, ball or scheme in the game sample: a slow NFL first step may reflect stunts, two-gap duties or slide protection
